prompt: What is `error` in Go?
hint: `go doc builtin.error` printed its whole declaration.

choices.text: A keyword that marks a function as able to throw
choices.why: Go has no throw, and `error` is not a keyword: it is a type the language declares.

choices.text: A string holding the message
choices.why: The message comes from a method; the value itself can be any type, such as `*fs.PathError`.

choices.text: An interface with one method, `Error() string`
choices.why: Right. Any type with that method is an `error`, and nil means no error.

choices.text: A struct from the `errors` package with a message field
choices.why: It is predeclared, in the universe and not in a package, and it has no fields at all, only a method.

prompt: In `~/errors`, `err` was declared once, as `error`. Why did `%T` print `*fs.PathError` on one line and `*strconv.NumError` on another?
hint: An interface value has two words.

choices.text: `:=` redeclared `err` with a new type at the second call
choices.why: `:=` with an existing name only assigns it; `err` kept its type, `error`, throughout.

choices.text: `%T` prints the type stored inside the interface, and each call stored a different one
choices.why: Right. The variable's type is `error`; the type word inside it changes with what was stored.

choices.text: Go converts the error to the type of the function that returned it, so each call gives `err` a new type
choices.why: Nothing was converted. `os.Open` and `Atoi` each returned a pointer of their own type, wrapped in the `error` interface.

choices.text: `%T` reads the package name from the error's message
choices.why: The message of the first error never says `fs`; `%T` reads the type, not the text.

prompt: `fmt.Println(err)` printed `open notes.txt: no such file or directory`. Where did that text come from?
hint: `fmt` checks what kind of value it was handed.

choices.text: From the error's `Error` method, which `fmt` calls
choices.why: Right. Calling `err.Error()` directly printed the same text for the `Atoi` error.

choices.text: From the operating system, which prints it to the terminal
choices.why: The system reports a code; the sentence is assembled by `*fs.PathError` and printed by the program.

choices.text: From a field called `Message` that every error carries
choices.why: `error` has no fields; `PathError` has `Op`, `Path` and `Err`, and none of them is the whole sentence.

choices.text: From `fmt` itself, which knows the wording for each failure
choices.why: `fmt` knows nothing about files; it asks the value for its text.

prompt: A function reports that nothing went wrong by returning an `error` equal to `___`.
hint: The doc comment of the built-in type ends with it.

prompt: `n, err := strconv.Atoi("12a")` gave `n` the value 0. What should the caller conclude about that 0?
hint: Look at `err` first.

choices.text: That the text held the number zero
choices.why: That is the trap: `"0"` would give 0 with a nil error, and here the error is not nil.

choices.text: That `Atoi` returns 0 for text it partly understood
choices.why: It did not read `12` and stop; it refused the whole input, as its message says.

choices.text: Nothing: beside a non-nil error the value is not an answer
choices.why: Right. A function with two results returns two, and the first means nothing when the second is an error.

choices.text: That the conversion overflowed and was set to the zero value
choices.why: The error said `invalid syntax`, not a range problem; and in either case the 0 is no answer.

prompt: What does the block under `if err != nil` do in idiomatic Go?
hint: Lesson 19 recommended a shape for special cases.

choices.text: It catches the error so that the lines after the call run anyway, as a catch block would
choices.why: Nothing is caught: the error is already a value, and the lines after it are the success path.

choices.text: It retries the call until `err` becomes nil
choices.why: A retry is one possible way to handle an error, written by hand; it is not what the block means.

choices.text: It handles the failure and leaves, by returning or ending the program
choices.why: Right. The success path then runs down the left margin below it.

choices.text: It logs the error, and the function carries on
choices.why: Logging and carrying on is how `~/errors-ignore` sold a free ticket, only with a log line.

prompt: Lesson 19's price function answered a bad age with `-1`. Why does the version in `~/errors-idiom` return an `error` instead?
hint: What did `./price 8` print?

choices.text: Because Go refuses negative numbers as results
choices.why: Any `int` can be returned, `-1` included; lesson 19's version compiled and ran.

choices.text: Because a failure then cannot pass for a price
choices.why: Right. A child's ticket is a real 0, and a stand-in number only works while every caller remembers it.

choices.text: Because an `error` is faster to compare than an `int`
choices.why: Speed was never the reason; an interface comparison is not cheaper than an integer one.

choices.text: Because `os.Exit` needs an error to set the status
choices.why: `os.Exit` takes an `int`; `main` chose 1 itself after seeing the error.

prompt: `./price -4 2>/dev/null; echo $?` printed only `1`. What does that show?
hint: `2>` names one of the program's outputs.

choices.text: That `price` accepted `-4` and printed nothing, so the run succeeded
choices.why: An accepted age prints a price and exits with 0, as `./price 30` did.

choices.text: That redirecting to `/dev/null` changed the exit status from 0 to 1
choices.why: Redirecting an output never changes the status; the same run without it also gave 1.

choices.text: That the message went to standard output
choices.why: Then it would still be on the screen; only standard error was thrown away.

choices.text: That it failed, and the message went to standard error
choices.why: Right. The message is for a person; a script reads the status.

prompt: In `~/errors-ignore` both errors were discarded with `_`. What did `go run . thirty` print?
hint: A failed `Atoi` returns a number anyway.

choices.text: `strconv.Atoi: parsing "thirty": invalid syntax`
choices.why: That message only appears when something prints the error, and `_` threw it away.

choices.text: `0`, a child's free ticket
choices.why: Right. `Atoi` returned 0 beside its error, and 0 went into `price` as an age.

choices.text: Nothing, because the program panicked
choices.why: A discarded error does not stop anything; the program carried on and printed a price.

choices.text: `20`, the adult price, because the age was never set
choices.why: The age was set, to the 0 that `Atoi` returned, and 0 is under 12.

prompt: In `main`, after `age, err := strconv.Atoi(...)`, the line `p, err ___ price(age, false)` compiles because `p` is new and `err` is only assigned.
hint: Lesson 5's rule about several names on the left.

prompt: Put the lines of one step of the idiom in the order they appear in `main`.
hint: Call, test, leave, and only then use the value.

prompt: What makes `*LineError` usable as an `error`?
hint: Count the methods `error` asks for.

choices.text: A line `implements error` beside the type
choices.why: Go has no `implements`; nothing in `~/errors-custom` declares it.

choices.text: Embedding the `error` type in the struct
choices.why: The struct has only `Line` and `Msg`; nothing is embedded.

choices.text: Being declared in the `errors` package
choices.why: It is declared in `main`, and the error types of section 02 live in `io/fs` and `strconv`.

choices.text: Its method `Error() string`
choices.why: Right. Having the one method is the whole requirement.

prompt: When is a type of your own, like `LineError`, worth writing rather than a plain message?
hint: Who reads the fields?

choices.text: Whenever a function can fail, so that every error it returns has a type of its own
choices.why: Every error already has a type; `price` failed with a sentence and needed nothing more.

choices.text: When the caller needs data about the failure, such as the line number
choices.why: Right. The fields carry the data and the `Error` method builds the message from them.

choices.text: When the message is longer than one line
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it; `line 2: no = in host localhost` is one short line.

choices.text: Only when the error has to stop the program
choices.why: Whether the program stops is the caller's decision, whatever the error's type.

prompt: In `~/errors-nil`, `check` returned `nil` and `load` returned that as an `error`. Why was `err == nil` false?
hint: An interface value has two words.

choices.text: Because `check` returned a pointer to an empty `LineError`
choices.why: The pointer was nil; nothing was allocated, which is why calling `Error` dereferenced nil.

choices.text: Because `go vet` changed the value before the run
choices.why: `go vet` only reads code, and it found nothing to say.

choices.text: Because the stored nil `*LineError` fills the type word
choices.why: Right. The interface held `*main.LineError` and a nil pointer, and it is nil only when both are empty.

choices.text: Because `nil` of one package is never equal to `nil` of another
choices.why: There is no per-package nil; the type stored in the interface is what differs.

prompt: A colleague's `func find(id int) *NotFound` returns `nil` on success, and callers write `err := find(id)` then `if err != nil`. Which changes stop a caller from seeing a failure that did not happen? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where does the typed nil get into an interface?

choices.text: Declare the result of `find` as `error` and return a literal `nil`
choices.why: Yes: that is the repair of `~/errors-nilfix`, a nil interface from the start.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as callers use `err :=`, because then `err` is a `*NotFound`
choices.why: That caller is safe today, but the first one that passes `err` on as an `error`, like `load`, sees a failure.

choices.text: Run `go vet`, which reports the typed nil
choices.why: `go vet && go run .` ran the program in `~/errors-nil`: vet reported nothing.

choices.text: Give `Error` a value receiver instead of a pointer receiver
choices.why: The receiver is not the problem: any nil `*NotFound` stored in an `error` still fills the type word.

prompt: Match each value stored in `var err error` to what `err == nil` gives.
hint: Both words empty, or not.

prompt: A function opens a file, and when `os.Open` fails it does `log.Println(err)` and goes on to read from the `*os.File` it got. What is wrong with that?
hint: What was `f` in `~/errors` when the file was missing?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the error is logged somewhere
choices.why: Logging tells a person; the function still goes on with a value that is no answer.

choices.text: Beside a non-nil error the `*os.File` is `nil`, so the function carries on with no file
choices.why: Right. `~/errors` printed `<nil>` for the file; the block should leave, not log and continue.

choices.text: `log.Println` cannot print an `error`
choices.why: It prints it like `fmt.Println` does, by calling `Error`.

choices.text: Go stops the function at the failed `os.Open`, so the read never runs
choices.why: Nothing stops by itself; the failure is a value, and the lines after it run unless the code leaves.

prompt: `parse(s string) (int, error)` reads a temperature, and every `int` is a possible temperature, negatives included. A teammate proposes returning `-9999` on bad input instead of an error. What is the strongest objection?
hint: The child's free ticket in section 03.

choices.text: Negative numbers cannot be returned from a function that also returns an `error`
choices.why: Any `int` can be returned beside an error; the problem is what the number means.

choices.text: `-9999` is too slow to compare
choices.why: Comparing integers costs nothing worth mentioning; speed was never the objection.

choices.text: Go programs never use special values
choices.why: Some do, like the `-1` of lesson 19; it is a habit that works only while a number is left over.

choices.text: It is a legal temperature, so a caller cannot tell a failure from a reading, and nothing forces anybody to check
choices.why: Right. When every value is an answer there is no number left to mean failed; an `error` beside it is unmistakable.

prompt: Counted over `/usr/local/go/src` with tests left out, how many lines of Go 1.27.1's standard library contain `if err != nil`?
hint: Section 03 opened with the count.

prompt: Which of these are true of an `error` in Go? Choose all that apply.
hint: Sections 02 and 04.

choices.text: It is an interface value: a type and a pointer
choices.why: Yes. Lesson 22 measured 16 bytes, and `%T` reads the type half.

choices.text: Returning one makes the caller's next lines skip until a handler
choices.why: That is an exception; an error is a value, and the caller's next line runs.

choices.text: `if err { }` does not compile
choices.why: Yes: `non-boolean condition in if statement`, the refusal of lesson 8.

choices.text: Its message is stored in a field that `fmt` reads
choices.why: `fmt` calls the `Error` method; `LineError` builds the text from `Line` and `Msg` each time.
